title: How the Innocence Project Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the Innocence Project, the New York-based (Benjamin N. Cardozo School of Law, Yeshiva University) group founded by Barry Scheck and Peter Neufeld that uses DNA evidence to exonerate wrongly convicted prisoners, with help from law students and, at Northwestern, journalism students. They cover the main causes of wrongful conviction (eyewitness misidentification and the other-race effect, improper forensic science, false confessions, jailhouse snitches), the Florida Bill Dillon case in Brevard County, the statistics on DNA exonerations and death row, evidence-preservation laws and the Justice for All Act, and close with a listener email from Becca.

segments.title: What the Innocence Project does
segments.summary: The Innocence Project, founded by Barry Scheck and Peter Neufeld and part of Benjamin Cardozo School of Law at Yeshiva University, uses DNA evidence to free wrongly imprisoned people, with law and sometimes journalism students investigating cases. Out of 254 DNA exonerations, the actual perpetrator was identified in 111.
topics: Benjamin N. Cardozo School of Law

segments.title: Why legal flaws matter and police misconduct
segments.summary: Hosts explain why law students are needed for post-conviction innocence appeals and discuss police misconduct, including the LAPD CRASH unit scandal that overturned between 100 and 150 convictions.

segments.title: Causes of wrongful conviction: eyewitnesses and forensics
segments.summary: Eyewitness misidentification figures in 70 percent of post-conviction DNA exonerations, linked to the other-race effect. Improper or unvetted forensic science, such as bite marks and hair microscopy, played a role in 50 percent of cases.

segments.title: False confessions and jailhouse snitches
segments.summary: False confessions occurred in many cases, often from defendants aged 18 or younger or developmentally disabled, as in the Victoria Banks case. Pressure to plead to escape jail while awaiting trial is discussed. Snitches were a factor in 19 percent of cases.

segments.title: Bill Dillon case in Brevard County
segments.summary: Bill Dillon was convicted of the 1981 beating death of James Dvorak on Canova Beach. Testimony came from a prison snitch, a witness who was blind in one eye, a girlfriend who had a relationship with the lead investigator, and a scent dog handler John Preston whose dog identified Dillon. Dillon served 26 years before a preserved T-shirt was DNA tested and exonerated him.

segments.title: Death row exonerations, lost evidence, and evidence-preservation laws
segments.summary: Statistics on exonerations (17 death row cases, two cases closed due to lost evidence), a 2004 study on death row exonerations, the Innocence Movement, and the Innocence Project's review of inmate letters. Only about half of states require preserving evidence after conviction; the federal Justice for All Act offers financial incentives. Scheck's goal of proving a wrongful execution is noted.
